questions.q: In Salesforce's modern Files model, what connects a ContentDocument to the record it's attached to?
options: ParentId, directly on the ContentDocument
The Attachment object
ContentDocumentLink
A standard lookup field called AttachedTo
questions.explain: ContentDocumentLink is what connects a ContentDocument (the file's identity) to the record(s) it belongs to. ParentId is how the older, legacy Attachment object links to its parent instead.

questions.q: What makes a file fundamentally different from a normal structured record for migration purposes?
options: A file carries binary content (the actual bytes) alongside its metadata, not just a row of field values, and is typically far larger per item
Files cannot be migrated into Salesforce under any circumstances
Files are always smaller in total data volume than structured records
Files never need to be linked to a parent record
questions.explain: Unlike text, numbers, or picklist values, a file's binary payload has to travel alongside its metadata, and that payload is typically much larger per item than a structured record's field values — which is why it needs different handling.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say file migration is usually planned as its own workstream rather than folded into the main structured-data load?
options: Because Salesforce technically forbids files and records from loading in the same project
Because of the size difference per item and because files are commonly the least standardized part of a legacy system
Because files never need to be attached to any parent record
Because ContentVersion records cannot be created through Bulk API or Data Loader
questions.explain: Files are typically much larger per item than structured records and tend to be less standardized (naming drift, duplicates, some no longer retrievable), which is why they're usually scoped, sequenced, and timed as a separate pass.

questions.q: A source system's files can only be downloaded one at a time through a web UI, with no bulk export API. Which of these does this lesson present as a legitimate option in that situation?
options: Immediately abandoning the entire migration project
Assuming the extraction will work exactly like the structured-data load, with no changes to the plan
Forcing all files into the legacy Attachment object instead of ContentVersion
Keeping the legacy system available read-only so files can still be retrieved after structured data cuts over, or building a scripted extraction and accepting a longer timeline
questions.explain: Legitimate options include a phased/parallel approach keeping the legacy system read-only for ongoing file retrieval, a scripted extraction accepting a longer timeline, or a deliberate scope decision to archive lower-value files rather than migrate them.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say file scope deserves its own conversation, separate from the main migration scope discussion in Lesson 4?
options: Because files are never actually part of migration scope
Because Salesforce limits every org to a fixed number of files regardless of scope
Because a blanket "migrate everything" decision on files specifically can balloon migration duration and storage cost for little business value if many files are old, unused, or duplicated
Because files must always be excluded from any migration by default
questions.explain: Because files are large and often poorly curated in a legacy system, deciding to migrate 'everything' without a specific files scope conversation can add significant time and storage cost for files that may provide little ongoing value.
